title: Metabolic and Nutritional Neurological Diseases
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how systemic metabolic problems injure the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves: ammonia in liver failure, hyperglycemia in diabetes, missing vitamin B12 or thiamine, and a sodium level corrected too fast. It also classifies peripheral neuropathy and covers Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, the commonest inherited neuropathy. Board questions usually describe a pattern of deficits and ask for the biochemical cause, the tract or nerve involved, or the trigger. If you can connect each enzyme or osmotic failure to the cells that need it most, the findings follow logically.
prerequisites: Urea cycle, glutamine synthetase, and ammonia handling in liver, muscle, and kidney
Cofactor roles of thiamine pyrophosphate, methylcobalamin, and adenosylcobalamin (NE-14)
Myelin, Schwann cells, oligodendrocytes, and saltatory conduction (NE-2, NE-13)
Dorsal column and corticospinal tract anatomy (NE-5, NE-7)
Course of the oculomotor nerve and the autonomic supply of the pupil and viscera (NE-8, NE-9)

connections.how: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension create the portosystemic shunting that lets gut-derived ammonia reach the brain.
Gastric and ileal disease, bariatric surgery, and pancreatic insufficiency explain most acquired B12 and thiamine deficiency.
B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia through the same methionine synthase failure that contributes to cord injury.
Guillain-Barre syndrome and multiple sclerosis are the immune counterparts to the metabolic and inherited demyelination taught here.
Renal ammoniagenesis, potassium balance, and water handling explain hypokalemic encephalopathy and the osmotic injury of rapid sodium correction.

terms.def: Reversible brain dysfunction caused by liver insufficiency or portosystemic shunting, mainly through ammonia and other gut-derived toxins.
Negative myoclonus: brief lapses of postural muscle tone that make outstretched, dorsiflexed hands flap.
Neuropathy that affects the longest axons first, producing stocking-glove sensory loss that begins in the feet.
Damage to two or more separately named nerves at different sites and times, typically from ischemia of the vasa nervorum.
Loss of myelin from individual internodes with the axon preserved, which slows or blocks conduction.
Reduction of glucose to sorbitol by aldose reductase using NADPH, followed by slow oxidation of sorbitol to fructose.
Irreversible adducts formed when glucose reacts nonenzymatically with proteins, which cross-link matrix and activate the receptor for AGEs (RAGE).
Vacuolar demyelination of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts caused by vitamin B12 deficiency.
Loss of balance when a patient stands with feet together and eyes closed, indicating impaired proprioception rather than cerebellar disease.
Production of false memories without intent to deceive, typical of Korsakoff syndrome.
Small solutes such as myo-inositol, taurine, and glutamine that brain cells shed or accumulate to defend their volume.
Concentric layers of Schwann cell processes around an axon, produced by repeated demyelination and remyelination.

sections.title: Hepatic encephalopathy: ammonia, precipitants, and asterixis

blocks.text: Ammonia is produced mainly in the gut. Colonic bacteria split urea and dietary protein with urease and deaminases, and small intestinal enterocytes release ammonia when glutaminase breaks down glutamine. Portal blood carries it to the liver, where periportal hepatocytes convert it to urea and perivenous hepatocytes trap the remainder as glutamine. Skeletal muscle also takes up ammonia through glutamine synthetase, so muscle wasting in cirrhosis removes a second buffer.

In cirrhosis, two defects coexist: fewer functioning hepatocytes and portosystemic collaterals (or a surgical or transjugular shunt) that carry portal blood straight into the systemic circulation. Ammonia, mercaptans, manganese, and other gut-derived compounds reach the brain. Uncharged NH3 diffuses across the blood-brain barrier, and astrocytes, which lack a urea cycle, detoxify it with glutamine synthetase.

blocks.title: From the gut to the astrocyte
steps: Gut bacteria and enterocytes generate ammonia
Failing liver and shunts let ammonia bypass urea synthesis
NH3 crosses the blood-brain barrier
Astrocyte glutamine synthetase forms glutamine
Glutamine draws in water; astrocytes swell and malfunction
Neurotransmission shifts toward inhibition: confusion, asterixis, coma
blocks.caption: Low-grade astrocyte swelling dominates in cirrhosis; in acute liver failure the same process can cause cerebral edema and herniation.

blocks.text: Glutamine is osmotically active, and its transport into astrocyte mitochondria generates ammonia and oxidative stress there. Swollen astrocytes handle glutamate and potassium poorly, and the brain shifts toward inhibition through increased GABAergic tone (partly from neurosteroids made by astrocytes). Systemic inflammation acts synergistically with ammonia, and manganese deposition in the basal ganglia adds parkinsonian features.

Each precipitant raises ammonia production, increases its entry into the brain, or adds sedation. Ammonia exists as NH4+ and NH3 with a pKa of about 9.2, so alkalosis shifts more toward diffusible NH3.

blocks.title: Precipitants of hepatic encephalopathy and their mechanisms
rows: Blood in the gut is a large protein load digested to ammonia; hypovolemia also lowers hepatic perfusion
Cytokines amplify ammonia neurotoxicity and increase blood-brain barrier permeability
More substrate for bacterial and enterocyte ammonia production
Longer colonic transit allows more bacterial ammonia production and absorption
Raises proximal tubule ammoniagenesis and causes metabolic alkalosis, favoring NH3
Hypokalemia, alkalosis, and prerenal azotemia (more urea diffusing into the gut)
Enhance the already increased GABA-A inhibitory tone
Diverts more portal blood around the liver
blocks.caption: Ask whether the trigger adds nitrogen, adds NH3 transfer into the brain, or adds inhibition.

blocks.text: Findings range from subtle inattention and reversal of the sleep-wake cycle to confusion, somnolence, and coma, graded 1 to 4 (West Haven criteria). Asterixis appears in the intermediate grades: when the patient holds the arms out with wrists dorsiflexed, brief losses of tone let the hands drop and recover. It reflects disordered motor control rather than a muscle problem, and it is not specific, appearing in uremia and carbon dioxide retention. Fetor hepaticus, a musty breath odor from sulfur-containing compounds, may be present. Blood ammonia supports the diagnosis but correlates only loosely with severity.

blocks.title: Why low potassium worsens encephalopathy
blocks.text: A patient with cirrhosis on a loop diuretic becomes confused with a serum K+ of 2.9 mEq/L (reference about 3.5 to 5.0). Potassium leaves cells in exchange for H+, so proximal tubule cells become relatively acidic, which stimulates glutaminase and ammonia production; more ammonia enters the renal vein. Volume loss and hypokalemia also generate metabolic alkalosis. At higher blood pH, a larger fraction of total ammonia is uncharged NH3, which diffuses into the brain more easily. Ammonia generation and brain entry both rise even though protein intake is unchanged.

sections.title: Classifying peripheral neuropathy by pattern and type of injury

blocks.text: Peripheral neuropathy is classified by the pattern of nerves involved and by whether the axon or the myelin is injured; together these narrow the cause.
Patterns

Distal symmetric polyneuropathy is length dependent. A neuron must synthesize and transport proteins and mitochondria along its entire axon, so systemic metabolic, toxic, and nutritional insults fail the longest axons first. Symptoms begin in the toes and rise to the knees before the fingers are affected, giving a stocking-glove distribution, and ankle reflexes are lost early. A mononeuropathy affects one nerve, usually from compression at a fixed site or focal ischemia. Mononeuritis multiplex affects several separately named nerves at random sites, often stepwise, most often because vasculitis of the vasa nervorum infarcts nerve segments supplied by different vessels; with time the lesions can merge and mimic a symmetric neuropathy.
Axonal versus demyelinating injury

In axonal injury, the axon degenerates distal to the damage (Wallerian degeneration after a focal lesion, distal dying back in metabolic disease). Fewer fibers conduct, so the amplitude of the compound action potential falls, while the surviving fibers conduct at nearly normal speed. Recovery requires regrowth at about 1 mm per day and is slow and often incomplete. In demyelinating injury, internodes lose myelin while axons survive, so saltatory conduction slows or fails; conduction velocity falls, distal latencies lengthen, and focal conduction block may appear. Remyelination can restore function within weeks. Uniform slowing along every nerve suggests an inherited myelin disorder, whereas patchy slowing with conduction block suggests an acquired immune attack.

blocks.title: Major causes of peripheral neuropathy
rows: Distal symmetric; also mononeuropathy and autonomic
Axonal; direct toxicity plus thiamine and other nutritional deficiency
Distal symmetric sensory, with cord disease
Axonal; energy failure in long axons
Axonal; ischemic infarction of nerve segments
Mononeuritis multiplex or patchy sensory loss in cool skin
Bacilli invade Schwann cells; granulomas in thickened nerves
Painful distal symmetric sensory neuropathy; less often demyelinating or multifocal
Mainly axonal; viral, inflammatory, and older antiretroviral toxicity
Axonal; microtubule disruption or dorsal root ganglion toxicity
blocks.caption: Most metabolic and toxic neuropathies are axonal and length dependent; ischemia gives multifocal axonal loss; immune and inherited myelin disorders are demyelinating (C06).

blocks.text: Leprosy deserves a note on mechanism. M. leprae grows best below core body temperature and binds Schwann cells through laminin on their basal lamina, so it damages nerves near the skin surface (ulnar, common fibular, great auricular), which become palpably thickened. Tuberculoid disease, with strong Th1 immunity, damages a few nerves beside hypopigmented anesthetic patches; lepromatous disease, with weak cell-mediated immunity, causes widespread symmetric sensory loss. Vincristine blocks microtubule assembly and taxanes freeze microtubules, and either way fast axonal transport to the distal axon fails.

Diabetic neuropathy is the commonest neuropathy in developed countries. Schwann cells, neurons, and endothelial cells take up glucose through insulin-independent transporters, so intracellular glucose rises with blood glucose. Several pathways then convert excess glucose into injury.

blocks.title: The polyol pathway in Schwann cells
steps: Hyperglycemia raises glucose inside Schwann cells
Aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol, using NADPH
Low sorbitol dehydrogenase activity traps sorbitol
Sorbitol draws in water; myo-inositol and Na+/K+-ATPase activity fall
NADPH loss limits glutathione regeneration; oxidative stress rises
Schwann cells and axons degenerate, longest fibers first
blocks.caption: The same pathway contributes to diabetic cataract and retinopathy in the lens and retina.

blocks.text: Advanced glycation end products form when glucose binds proteins nonenzymatically. They cross-link collagen and basement membrane, and their receptor (RAGE) activates NF-kB and generates reactive oxygen species. Hyperglycemia also activates protein kinase C through diacylglycerol. Together these thicken the basement membrane of endoneurial capillaries and narrow the vasa nervorum, so endoneurial blood flow falls and the nerve becomes hypoxic. Metabolic injury explains the slow symmetric neuropathy; acute vascular occlusion explains the sudden mononeuropathies.

blocks.title: Diabetic neuropathy syndromes explained by fiber type
rows: Small fibers (pain, temperature) early; large fibers (vibration, position) later
Burning feet, stocking-glove loss, lost ankle reflexes, sensory ataxia
Small myelinated and unmyelinated autonomic fibers
Gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension, fixed resting tachycardia, erectile dysfunction, neurogenic bladder, distal anhidrosis
Ischemic infarct of the nerve core
Pupil-sparing CN III palsy; CN VI palsy
Ischemic and inflammatory injury to roots and plexus
Painful asymmetric proximal thigh weakness and wasting
blocks.caption: The longest fibers of every type fail first, which is why the vagus and the sweat gland fibers of the feet are early autonomic targets.

blocks.text: Autonomic findings follow the lost efferents. Vagal damage slows gastric emptying and leaves the resting heart rate high and fixed. Damage to sympathetic vasoconstrictor fibers to the splanchnic and limb vessels prevents the reflex vasoconstriction that normally holds blood pressure on standing, giving orthostatic hypotension.

Neuropathic foot ulcers form under the metatarsal heads and heel because three losses combine. Without protective sensation, repeated pressure goes unnoticed. Motor loss of the intrinsic foot muscles produces claw toes that load the metatarsal heads. Sympathetic loss causes dry, cracked skin. Peripheral arterial disease then slows healing, and unfelt fractures can destroy the midfoot (Charcot neuroarthropathy).

In the oculomotor nerve, parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers run superficially and are supplied by surface pial vessels, while the core depends on penetrating vasa nervorum. Diabetic microvascular infarction of the core causes ptosis and a down-and-out eye with a normal pupil, often with pain, and usually recovers over about 3 months. A compressive lesion such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm presses on the surface first, so the pupil dilates early.

blocks.predict: A patient has sudden ptosis, a down-and-out eye, and a fixed dilated pupil. Is diabetic infarction the likely cause?
blocks.explain: No. Pupillary fibers lie on the surface of CN III with their own surface blood supply, so infarction of the core spares them. A dilated pupil indicates external compression, classically a posterior communicating artery aneurysm or uncal herniation.

sections.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency and subacute combined degeneration

blocks.text: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) comes only from animal foods. Absorption has several steps, and each named cause of deficiency breaks one of them. Stomach acid and pepsin free B12 from food protein; it binds haptocorrin (R binder) from saliva; pancreatic proteases digest haptocorrin in the duodenum; B12 then binds intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells; and the complex is absorbed by cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum. Transcobalamin carries it in plasma. The liver stores several milligrams, enough for about 3 to 5 years, so dietary deficiency develops slowly.

blocks.title: Causes of B12 deficiency by step
rows: Release from food and intrinsic factor
Pernicious anemia; gastrectomy or gastric bypass; atrophic gastritis; long-term acid suppression
Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm from raw freshwater fish); bacterial overgrowth in blind loops
Crohn disease of the terminal ileum, ileal resection; metformin reduces uptake
Nitrous oxide oxidizes cobalamin and inactivates methionine synthase
blocks.caption: Nitrous oxide can unmask marginal stores quickly.

blocks.text: Pernicious anemia is autoimmune gastritis of the gastric body and fundus. T cells and antibodies against the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase destroy parietal cells, causing achlorhydria and loss of intrinsic factor; antibodies to intrinsic factor are less sensitive but highly specific. Gastrin rises because acid no longer inhibits antral G cells. It is associated with other autoimmune diseases such as thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes.

B12 is a cofactor for two enzymes. Methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin to transfer a methyl group from N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, forming methionine (then S-adenosylmethionine, the main methyl donor) and regenerating tetrahydrofolate for DNA synthesis. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses adenosylcobalamin to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Deficiency therefore raises both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid (MMA) and causes megaloblastic anemia. Folate deficiency raises homocysteine but not MMA. How the nervous system is injured is not fully settled: reduced S-adenosylmethionine impairs methylation of myelin proteins and lipids, and accumulated methylmalonyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA may lead to abnormal fatty acids in myelin. Folate can correct the anemia but not the neurologic injury, so folate alone can mask B12 deficiency while the cord degenerates.

Subacute combined degeneration is vacuolar swelling and loss of myelin, then axons, in the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, usually beginning in the cervical and upper thoracic cord. Dorsal column loss removes vibration and joint position sense, so the patient relies on vision to balance and falls when the eyes close (positive Romberg sign) and walks with a broad-based sensory ataxia. Corticospinal loss gives spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses. A coexisting axonal neuropathy causes distal paresthesias and can abolish ankle reflexes. Cerebral involvement causes memory loss, depression, psychosis, or dementia, and optic neuropathy may occur. Neurologic signs can appear without anemia or macrocytosis.

blocks.title: Localizing a mixed upper and lower motor neuron picture
blocks.text: A 62-year-old with a partial gastrectomy has tingling feet, falls in the dark, absent ankle reflexes, brisk knee reflexes, and bilateral Babinski signs. Vibration is absent at the toes and reduced at the knees. Falling in the dark and lost vibration localize to large-fiber sensory pathways (dorsal columns and peripheral nerve). Babinski signs and brisk knee reflexes require corticospinal disease, while absent ankle reflexes reflect the peripheral neuropathy interrupting the longest reflex arc. One lesion cannot explain both, but B12 deficiency damages cord and nerve together. Raised MMA and homocysteine with low serum B12 (reference about 200 to 900 pg/mL) would confirm it.

Thiamine (vitamin B1) is converted to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway, and branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase. Without TPP, pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle and the cycle itself slows, so glucose oxidation and ATP production fail and lactate accumulates. The brain depends almost entirely on glucose oxidation, so it is vulnerable. Body stores are small (about 30 mg) and can be depleted in about 2 to 3 weeks of poor intake.

Alcohol use disorder is the commonest setting: diet is poor, alcohol reduces intestinal thiamine absorption, and liver disease impairs storage and conversion to TPP. Other causes are malnutrition, hyperemesis gravidarum and other prolonged vomiting, bariatric surgery, malignancy, and refeeding after starvation. A glucose load in a depleted patient increases flux through the thiamine-dependent steps and can precipitate or worsen an attack.

blocks.title: From thiamine depletion to Wernicke lesions
steps: Thiamine intake, absorption, or storage falls
TPP-dependent dehydrogenases and transketolase lose activity
Glucose oxidation fails; ATP falls and lactate rises
Ion gradients fail; cytotoxic edema and glutamate excitotoxicity
High-turnover periventricular regions are damaged first
Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia
blocks.caption: Damage is symmetric around the third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, and fourth ventricle.

blocks.text: Wernicke encephalopathy is the acute stage. Lesions involve the mammillary bodies, the medial (dorsomedial) thalamus, the periaqueductal gray, the oculomotor, abducens, and vestibular nuclei in the brainstem, and the superior cerebellar vermis. Acutely they show edema, endothelial swelling, and petechial hemorrhage; later the mammillary bodies shrink and contain hemosiderin. Only a minority of patients show the full triad, so any one feature in a malnourished patient should raise the question.

blocks.title: The Wernicke triad and its anatomy
rows: Medial thalamus, mammillary bodies, diffuse energy failure
Ophthalmoplegia: nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy, conjugate gaze palsy
Abducens and oculomotor nuclei, vestibular nuclei, gaze centers
Superior cerebellar vermis and vestibular dysfunction
blocks.caption: Eye findings and confusion are often reversible early; the ataxia and memory loss may persist.

blocks.text: Korsakoff syndrome is the chronic stage, usually following untreated or recurrent Wernicke encephalopathy. Damage to the mammillary bodies, the mammillothalamic tract, and the anterior and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei interrupts the diencephalic memory circuits, including the Papez circuit, that consolidate new declarative memories. The result is severe anterograde amnesia, variable retrograde amnesia, and confabulation, which fills gaps with false memories produced without intent to deceive. Attention, immediate recall, and other intellectual functions are relatively preserved, which distinguishes it from global dementia. It is largely irreversible because neurons have been lost.

Peripheral thiamine deficiency causes beriberi. Dry beriberi is an axonal, length-dependent sensorimotor neuropathy; wet beriberi is high-output heart failure from peripheral vasodilation as tissue energy fails.

blocks.predict: A malnourished man with vomiting is given intravenous glucose alone and within hours develops nystagmus and confusion. Why did glucose make him worse?
blocks.explain: Glucose increases flux toward pyruvate dehydrogenase and the TCA cycle, which require TPP. With little thiamine available, the load consumes what remains and the blocked steps fail completely in high-demand periventricular neurons.
blocks.check: The thiamine enzymes and precipitant paragraphs.

blocks.text: Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease, also called hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy, is a genetically diverse group of inherited neuropathies and the commonest inherited peripheral neuropathy. All forms are length dependent, so distal leg muscles weaken first, and all progress slowly, typically beginning in the first or second decade.

The most common form, CMT1A, is autosomal dominant and caused by a duplication on chromosome 17p12 that contains PMP22 (peripheral myelin protein 22). The extra copy raises PMP22 expression, a gene dosage effect, and the excess protein misfolds and destabilizes compact myelin. Schwann cells repeatedly demyelinate and remyelinate, layering their processes around axons as onion bulbs, so nerves can become palpably enlarged. Conduction slows uniformly in every nerve, unlike the patchy slowing of acquired demyelination, and secondary axonal loss eventually produces the weakness. Deletion of the same region produces the opposite dosage problem, hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies.

blocks.title: Main forms of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
blocks.caption: CMT1 means demyelinating and CMT2 means axonal; the clinical picture is similar.

blocks.text: The findings come from distal muscle imbalance. Weak tibialis anterior and fibular (peroneal) muscles cause foot drop, so the patient lifts the knee high to clear the toes (steppage gait) and trips easily. Wasting of the distal leg with preserved thigh bulk gives the inverted champagne bottle appearance. The intrinsic foot muscles weaken early; the long toe extensors and flexors then pull unopposed, clawing the toes into hammer toes. Relatively stronger fibularis longus and tibialis posterior acting against weaker antagonists raise and invert the arch, giving pes cavus. Ankle reflexes are reduced or absent, and distal sensory loss is usually mild compared with the weakness. Hands become involved later.

Water crosses cell membranes freely, so a fall in plasma osmolality from hyponatremia drives water into brain cells. Within hours the brain limits swelling by exporting Na+, K+, and Cl-. Over about 48 hours it also sheds organic osmolytes such as myo-inositol, taurine, glutamine, and glutamate, which returns cell volume nearly to normal. Hyponatremia present this long is called chronic, and the adapted brain tolerates it relatively well.

Restoring osmolytes takes days, much longer than losing them. If serum sodium is then raised quickly, extracellular osmolality rises before the cells can rebuild their osmolyte content, so water leaves and the cells shrink. Shrinkage disrupts endothelial tight junctions and the blood-brain barrier, and oligodendrocytes undergo apoptosis, stripping myelin while neurons and axons are relatively spared. Risk rises when sodium increases by more than about 10 to 12 mEq/L in 24 hours, and lower thresholds apply to high-risk patients: those with a starting sodium of 105 mEq/L or less (reference about 135 to 145), alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, or advanced liver disease. The syndrome is rare when the starting sodium is above about 120 mEq/L.

blocks.title: How rapid correction demyelinates the pons
steps: Chronic hyponatremia: brain cells shed organic osmolytes
Serum sodium is raised too quickly
Water leaves cells faster than osmolytes return
Cells shrink; blood-brain barrier is disrupted
Oligodendrocytes in the central pons die
Days later: quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia
blocks.caption: The same mechanism explains extrapontine lesions in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and cerebellum.

blocks.text: The central basis pontis is most vulnerable, possibly because its many oligodendrocytes lie interwoven with gray matter in the pontine nuclei; extrapontine lesions are common, with or without pontine involvement. The course is biphasic: the confusion of hyponatremia improves as sodium rises, then about 2 to 6 days later the patient deteriorates. Corticobulbar fiber loss produces dysarthria, dysphagia, and pseudobulbar palsy; corticospinal loss produces quadriparesis that is flaccid early and spastic later. A large lesion of the basis pontis that spares the tegmentum produces locked-in syndrome, in which the patient is awake and aware, because the reticular activating system is intact, but can move only the eyes vertically and blink. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a symmetric central pontine T2 hyperintensity that spares the periphery, often appearing a week or two after symptoms.

blocks.predict: Why does raising sodium by 15 mEq/L in 24 hours cause demyelination in a patient whose hyponatremia developed over 3 weeks, but not in one whose hyponatremia developed over 6 hours?
blocks.explain: After 3 weeks the brain has shed organic osmolytes and cannot regain them quickly, so rapid correction shrinks its cells. After 6 hours, swelling has been opposed mainly by electrolyte shifts that reverse quickly, so the brain is still swollen and correction restores normal volume.
blocks.check: The osmolyte adaptation and correction paragraphs.

integration.text: Each disease in this chapter is a biochemical or osmotic failure in the cells that depend most on the missing function. Astrocytes alone detoxify brain ammonia, so they swell in liver failure. Periventricular regions around the third ventricle, aqueduct, and fourth ventricle have the highest thiamine-dependent oxidative turnover, so Wernicke lesions cluster there. Cobalamin-dependent methylation and odd-chain metabolism support myelin, so B12 deficiency strikes the long myelinated tracts of the cord and nerves. The longest axons have the greatest transport and energy burden, so diabetic, alcoholic, toxic, and inherited neuropathies begin in the feet. Oligodendrocytes in the pons fail when cell volume changes faster than osmolytes can follow.

Overlapping findings are separated by mechanism. Confusion with asterixis suggests metabolic encephalopathy from liver, kidney, or carbon dioxide retention; confusion with ophthalmoplegia suggests thiamine deficiency; dorsal column loss with corticospinal signs suggests B12 deficiency, copper deficiency, or nitrous oxide exposure. Nerve conduction studies separate axonal from demyelinating neuropathy, but many disorders are mixed. Blood ammonia, serum B12, and imaging all correlate imperfectly with severity, so they support rather than replace the clinical pattern.

summary: In cirrhosis, gut ammonia bypasses the urea cycle; astrocytes convert it to glutamine, swell, and shift the brain toward inhibition.
GI bleeding, infection, protein load, constipation, hypokalemia with alkalosis, and sedatives precipitate hepatic encephalopathy; asterixis is negative myoclonus.
Length-dependent neuropathy gives stocking-glove loss; mononeuritis multiplex reflects vasa nervorum ischemia, as in vasculitis.
Axonal injury lowers conduction amplitude and recovers slowly; demyelination slows conduction velocity and can recover quickly.
Diabetic neuropathy results from sorbitol accumulation with NADPH loss, AGEs, and microvascular injury; the pupil is spared in diabetic CN III infarction.
B12 deficiency raises homocysteine and methylmalonic acid and causes subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, even without anemia.

Thiamine deficiency impairs PDH, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase; Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) can progress to Korsakoff amnesia with confabulation.
CMT1A is an autosomal dominant PMP22 duplication causing uniform demyelination, foot drop, pes cavus, and hammer toes.
Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia shrinks osmolyte-depleted brain cells and demyelinates the central pons, causing quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia, or locked-in syndrome.

verify: Thiamine body stores (about 30 mg) and the time to depletion (about 2 to 3 weeks) vary among sources; values are given as approximate.
The fraction of Wernicke patients with the complete triad is often quoted near 10% to 20% from autopsy series; the chapter says only a minority.
Sodium correction thresholds linked to osmotic demyelination differ among guidelines (about 8, 10 to 12 mEq/L in 24 hours, or 18 mEq/L in 48 hours); confirm the figure NABNE expects.
The mechanism of B12-related myelin injury (impaired methylation versus abnormal fatty acids from methylmalonyl-CoA) is unsettled; confirm which explanation NABNE favors.
Hepatic B12 stores lasting about 3 to 5 years is a commonly quoted range; some texts give longer.
Reference ranges for serum B12 (about 200 to 900 pg/mL), sodium, and potassium vary between laboratories.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the West Haven grading, the Papez circuit name, and the eponym inverted champagne bottle, or only the descriptive findings.
The proportion of osmotic demyelination with extrapontine lesions varies widely between series (from about 10% to about half); the chapter gives no figure.
